meaning: She who causes the throat to breathe

pronunciation.ipaLabel: Conventional reading — Egyptian vocalisation not attested

phonemes.desc: Written srqt; the name is usually explained as “she who causes the throat to breathe” (s + rḳ + t).
Conventionally vocalised “Serket”; the q is a voiceless uvular stop.

pronunciation.note: Her name is a sentence: the scorpion-goddess as the one who lets the poisoned throat breathe again. The final -t is the feminine ending.

domains.title: Goddess of Scorpions, Poison, and the Protection of the Vulnerable
domains.subtitle: She Who Causes the Throat to Breathe
domains.lead: Srqt — Serket — is the scorpion’s sting turned to medicine: the goddess of venom and its cure. She guards the vulnerable — children, the poisoned, the dead in their most helpless passage — and her scorpion crawls at the feet of kings and coffins alike, holding the poison at bay by its mere presence.

cards.name: Mistress of Poison
cards.desc: Commander of the scorpion’s sting; her priests were the healers of venom bites.

cards.name: Guardian of the Dead
cards.desc: One of the four goddesses protecting the canopic chest and the sarcophagus itself.

cards.name: Protector of Children
cards.desc: Her amulets warded nurseries; the scorpion on a wall meant “no venom enters here”.

cards.name: The Breathing Throat
cards.desc: Her name is a cure: she who lets the constricted throat of the stung breathe again.

mythology.lead: Serket is a guardian more than a protagonist: she appears wherever protection is most needed, arms outspread over the thing she shields. Her mythic presence clusters around the dying god — she is one of the four goddesses of the canopic equipment in the Osiris cycle — and around the threatened child, above all the young Horus hidden in the Chemmis marshes.

myths.title: The Four Guardians of the Dead
myths.text: When Isis wrapped the reassembled Osiris, the four great protective goddesses — Isis, Nephthys, Neith and Serket — took station at the corners of his bier and canopic chest. Serket’s scorpion stands for the poisoned threats of the night that must be kept from the god’s body; her arms spread in the ‘Isis-knot’ gesture frame every royal sarcophagus hall.

myths.title: The Scorpion and the Child Horus
myths.text: The great cippi of Horus the child — the Metternich Stela above all — tell how the infant god was stung by a scorpion in the marshes and revived by the divine mother's magic. Serket stands within that cycle as the power over the venom itself: the sting belongs to her, and so, therefore, does its antidote.

myths.title: The Scorpion of the King
myths.text: From the earliest dynasties the scorpion guarded the king’s name — King Scorpion of the Predynastic period took the animal as his emblem — and Serket’s image walked at the prow and stern of the royal barque. Her presence converts the desert’s deadliest small killer into a bodyguard.

myths.title: She Who Waits at the Head of the Bier
myths.text: In the tomb, Serket and her three sisters stand at the four sides of the sarcophagus, each uttering protection: ‘I am Serket, I encircle with my protection.’ Her protection is specifically against poison and bite — the everyday killers of the Nile valley made powerless at the moment of greatest vulnerability.

lore.syncretism: Serket was early fused with the greater scorpion-powers of the pantheon and by the New Kingdom is barely separable from Isis in her protective aspect; some temples give her a healing consort-form of Horus. The Greeks called her Selkis and kept her as a goddess of the dead; her name entered the magical papyri of late antiquity as a power-word against poison.
lore.culturalLegacy: Her image — woman with a scorpion on her head, arms winged out in protection — is one of the most immediately readable Egyptian glyphs of care. The Metternich Stela and the Horus cippi made her the patroness of a whole genre of healing magic that persisted into Coptic exorcistic texts.
lore.extendedMeditation: Srqt is a name that performs its function: read it, and the throat opens. The scorpion-goddess guards this page as she guarded the bier — quietly, at the corners, with poison turned outward. Plain letters are her amulet: nothing decorative survives translation, but the protection does.

sources.name: Serket entries in Lexikon der Ägyptologie

lore.archaeology: She stands at the corners of Tutankhamun’s canopic shrine — the gilded goddesses of the treasury are among the most photographed objects of Egypt — and in relief on royal sarcophagi from the Old Kingdom onward. Her scorpion emblem marks protective amulets by the thousand in museum collections.
lore.cult: Her healing cult was practical: priests of Serket were invoked for scorpion stings and snakebite, and her stelae stood at settlement edges where the desert’s fauna met the fields. In the necropolis her cult was one of vigil — the eternal night-watch over the dead.
lore.iconography: A woman wearing a scorpion atop her head, arms extended in the protective gesture, sometimes winged; or the scorpion alone with a woman’s head. Her knot-gesture, two arms angled like the tit of Isis, frames coffins and doorways against the entry of venom.
lore.reception: Greek magicians adopted her into the Sethian-Typhonian protection formulae, and her scorpion remains a staple of Egyptological iconography studies as the clearest case of a dangerous animal wholly converted into a protective emblem.
